summary: Describes how to carry the UEMCLIP speech codec in RTP packets. UEMCLIP is an enhancement of ITU-T G.711 whose bitstream embeds a mu-law (PCMU) stream, so it is easy to convert to ordinary G.711. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: A voice recording can be sent in a plain version or a richer version that hides the plain one inside. This document explains how to pack that richer sound into Internet packets so phones can send it.

questions: how is uemclip carried in rtp
how does uemclip relate to g.711
subtitle: How to carry a G.711-compatible wideband speech codec in RTP packets, with the plain u-law stream tucked inside.

tldr.problem: Phones and conferencing bridges that only speak G.711 must coexist with wideband terminals, and converting between the two normally means costly decoding and re-encoding.
tldr.mechanism: UEMCLIP packs a G.711 u-law core layer and optional enhancement layers into each 20-ms frame, behind a 6-byte main header. This RFC defines how those frames ride in RTP and how modes are negotiated in SDP.
tldr.outcome: Going from UEMCLIP down to G.711 is just extracting the core layer. Going up from G.711 is limited to Mode 0, because enhancement layers cannot be generated.

today: RFC 5686 is a Proposed Standard, published in October 2009, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It registers the audio/UEMCLIP media subtype with IANA.

sections.title: What UEMCLIP Is For
sections.content:
RFC 5686 specifies the payload format for sending UEMCLIP (mU-law EMbedded Coder for Low-delay IP communication) speech over the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP). The RFC calls UEMCLIP a proprietary codec that enhances u-law ITU-T G.711, designed to ease the move toward wideband communication while keeping the transcoding load on existing terminals very small. Those terminals are ones in which G.711 is mandatory.

The embedded design does not help everywhere. Codecs are usually negotiated with SDP, and RTP mixers and translators may not transcode at all. The RFC points to a different case: Multi-point Control Units (MCUs) that terminate media and RTCP, where narrowband and wideband terminals coexist. There, the embedded bitstream turns transcoding into a simple bitstream truncation.

The document describes only the bitstream format, not how an encoder or decoder is implemented.
sections.eli5: Old phones only understand one kind of sound. UEMCLIP hides that old kind of sound inside a better one, so a meeting can include both old and new phones without much work.

sections.title: Layers and Modes
sections.content:
UEMCLIP works on 20-ms frames and has three sub-coders. Layer a is the G.711 u-law core at 64 kbit/s. Layer b is a lower-band quality enhancement at 16 kbit/s using time domain block quantization. Layer c is a higher-band enhancement at 16 kbit/s using MDCT block quantization.

Combining layers gives four modes. Mode 0 is the core alone at 8 kHz. Mode 1 is layers a and c at 16 kHz (80 kbit/s without headers). Mode 3 is layers a and b at 8 kHz (80 kbit/s). Mode 4 is all three layers at 16 kHz (96 kbit/s). Modes 2 and 5 are reserved for possible future 32 kHz modes, and any mode not in the table MUST NOT be used. Only single-channel operation is supported in this version.

Internal headers add overhead, so the total bit-rates are higher than the layer sums: 67.2, 84.0, 84.0 and 100.8 kbit/s for Modes 0, 1, 3 and 4. Implementations differ in which modes they support, so sender and receiver must negotiate.
sections.eli5: There is a basic layer that everyone can use, and two extras that make the sound clearer or fuller. Different phones can choose different combinations.

sections.title: The RTP Payload and Frames
sections.content:
An RTP packet carries the normal RTP header followed by one or more UEMCLIP frames. Each frame is a main header (MH) followed by up to three sub-layers (SLs). The core layer, Layer a, MUST always be present, but it may not come right after the MH, and the order of sub-layers is arbitrary. A decoder MUST therefore use the layer indices to decode correctly.

The bitstream does not say which mode or sampling frequency it uses. That information MUST be exchanged when the connection is set up, for example with SDP.

RTP header use is specific in a few places. The payload type is expected to be in the dynamic range. The timestamp MUST advance at 8000 or 16000 Hz, and if the sampling rate can change during a session it MUST use the maximum rate in the mode range and never change. The marker bit SHOULD be set on the first packet after a silence period when discontinuous transmission is used, and MUST be zero otherwise.

A packet may hold several frames, but frames MUST NOT be split between packets, all frames in a packet MUST share one mode, and a packet SHOULD NOT hold more frames than fit in the path MTU. Fewer frames per packet means lower delay.
sections.eli5: Each packet is a box holding one or more short slices of speech. A slice never gets cut between two boxes, and all slices in a box are the same kind.

sections.title: Main Header and Sub-Layers
sections.content:
The main header is 6 bytes: an 8-bit MX field (mixing information) and a 40-bit PC field (packet-loss concealment information). All numbers are in network byte order.

MX holds a check bit C1, a reserved bit, a voice activity flag V1 and a 5-bit power code PW1 computed from the RMS of Layer a. It is mainly meant for MCUs that mix streams. PC holds check bit C2, reserved bits, a second voice activity flag V2, a 4-bit frame indicator K (0 to 15) that says which earlier frame the extra parameters describe, voiced/unvoiced flags U1 and U2, 7-bit pitch codes P1 and P2, an 8-bit power code PW2 and 8 reserved bits. Pitch lag is the code plus 20 samples at 8 kHz, and codes 0x65 to 0x7F are not used. A check bit of 0 means the parameters should be ignored.

Each sub-layer starts with a sub-header: 2-bit channel index (CI), 2-bit frequency index (FI), 2-bit quality index (QI), 2 reserved bits and an 8-bit size SB, followed by SB*8 bits of layer data. Layer a has CI, FI, QI of 0, 0, 0. Layer b is 0, 0, 1. Layer c is 0, 1, 0.
sections.eli5: Every slice starts with a small label that tells how loud it is and whether it is speech, so a helper can mix voices or patch a lost piece. Each layer inside has its own tag saying what it is and how big it is.

sections.title: Transcoding To and From G.711
sections.content:
Because the u-law G.711 stream is always embedded as Layer a, converting UEMCLIP to G.711 needs no decode and re-encode. The transcoder finds the sub-layer whose layer index is 0x00 and takes its data, which is SB=160 bytes for a 20-ms frame. It should not assume the core layer sits right after the main header.

The reverse is harder. A G.711 stream has no enhancement layers, and the main header information must be assigned separately, so G.711 can only become Mode 0. A-law input should first be converted to u-law. The core layer MUST be a 160-sample chunk, C1 and C2 are set to 0, reserved bits take their defaults, and the sub-layer header has CI, FI, QI and R4 all 0 with SB equal to 160.

A transcoding device like this sits in the topologies of RFC 5117 and MUST rewrite RTCP packets together with the RTP media packets.
sections.eli5: Pulling the plain cracker out of the sandwich is easy. Making a sandwich from a lone cracker is not, because you have no extra layers to add.

sections.title: Media Type and SDP Negotiation
sections.content:
The RFC registers the media type audio/UEMCLIP. Its required rate parameter MUST be 8000 or 16000. Optional parameters are ptime, maxptime and mode, a comma-separated list drawn from 0, 1, 3 and 4. A single mode means the mode must not change during the session. The type is defined only for transfer over RTP.

In SDP, the m= line MUST be audio, and the a=rtpmap line uses the subtype name. Packet time SHOULD be a multiple of 20, defaulting to 20. An offerer lists acceptable modes in a=fmtp in descending priority, for example mode=4,1,3,0. If no mode is given, the payload type defaults to a single mode: Mode 0 at 8000 Hz and Mode 1 at 16000 Hz. Modes 1 and 4 cannot be used with a clock rate of 8000.

Offer-answer follows RFC 3264. The answerer MUST reply with a subset of the offered modes, unknown fmtp parameters MUST be ignored, and a single payload type is RECOMMENDED in the answer. Decoders SHOULD accept bitstreams in any mode, although an implementation may not cope with mode changes mid-session.
sections.eli5: Before talking, the two phones swap lists of the sound styles they can handle, best first. Then they agree on a style both can use.

sections.title: Security and Congestion Considerations
sections.content:
Packets are subject to the security considerations of RFC 3550 and its profiles, so confidentiality comes from encryption. The RFC notes the denial-of-service risk of codecs with uneven decoding cost, and says UEMCLIP does not show significant non-uniformity.

A separate risk is memory attacks through illegal layer indices or byte counts. A decoder implementer should assume the numbers may be corrupted and could point past the bitstream boundary, and it is advised to reject such layers.

For congestion, the general RTP rules apply. Dropping to a lower-rate mode reduces bandwidth, if dynamic mode changing was negotiated. Packing more frames per packet cuts IP/UDP/RTP header overhead but adds delay and reduces robustness to loss.
sections.eli5: Do not trust a label blindly, because a damaged one could send you looking in the wrong place. Also, bigger boxes save postage but arrive later.
